title: Resilience of the euro area economy – weathering one shock, preparing for the next
gist: ECB economists argue the euro area absorbed the 2026 Middle East energy shock with steady ~0.3% q/q growth (ex-Ireland) because oil intensity has halved since the early 1990s, renewables and nuclear have cut gas's role in setting power prices (Spain ~80% to ~20% of hours, France ~60% to ~20%), and temporary props helped: fiscal support doubled to 0.5pp, and AI lifted global trade and investment. They warn the cyclical supports (AI boom, fiscal stance, global demand) may fade, so future resilience depends on energy transition, grid integration, AI diffusion and a savings and investments union.

themes.theme: Growth held up through the 2026 shock

insights.claim: Excluding volatile Irish data, euro area real GDP in Q2 2026 was 0.6% above its Q4 2025 level, with a stable growth rate of around 0.3% quarter-on-quarter in each of the last four quarters, better than forecasts expected despite the 2026 energy price shock.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Euro area growth has not cracked under the energy shock, which reduces the odds of an emergency easing response and supports European cyclicals versus recession-priced positioning.
insights.quote: real GDP in the second quarter of 2026 was 0.6% above the level reached in the fourth quarter of 2025
insights.locator: A series of shocks

insights.claim: Since 2022 the euro area has absorbed a pandemic aftermath, the Russia-Ukraine energy crisis, Red Sea shipping disruptions and US tariff tensions without any shock producing outright declines in output, although growth has run below its long-term average.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A track record of shocks not turning into output contractions argues for fading recession calls on each new euro area shock, while accepting a low-growth trend.
insights.quote: Adverse shocks have not resulted in declines in output
insights.locator: A series of shocks

insights.claim: The ECB authors frame economic resilience as three complementary dimensions: absorptive capacity (limiting a shock's immediate impact), recovery capacity (returning quickly to the pre-shock path) and adaptive capacity (adjusting structures and institutions to cut vulnerability to future shocks).
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A useful lens for separating durable structural gains from temporary policy and AI-driven support when judging how much a resilient growth print should be extrapolated.
insights.quote: absorptive capacity, the ability to limit the immediate impact of a shock; recovery capacity, or the ability to return quickly to the pre-shock path; and adaptive capacity
insights.locator: The concept of economic resilience

insights.claim: The authors stress distinguishing lasting structural improvements in euro area resilience from support provided by policy measures and the AI-driven upswing, which may prove more temporary.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Part of the resilience is borrowed from cyclical tailwinds, so investors should not fully capitalise recent growth outperformance into longer-run euro area earnings assumptions.
insights.quote: support from policy measures and the AI-driven upswing, which may prove more temporary
insights.locator: The experience of the latest energy shock

insights.claim: The Middle East conflict initially sent oil prices soaring, prices eased after the June US-Iran memorandum of understanding, and then a second wave starting in July brought another significant oil price rise plus sharp increases in refining margins and a sustained rise in gas prices.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The 2026 energy shock came in two waves, with the second hitting refined products and gas as well as crude, which matters for refiners and for gas-sensitive European industry.
insights.quote: A second wave of the shock starting in July saw another significant increase in oil prices, along with sharp increases in refining margins and a sustained rise in gas prices.
insights.locator: Is the economy less vulnerable to energy shocks?

insights.claim: The euro area economy is only half as reliant on oil as it was in the early 1990s, measured as oil intensity per euro of real GDP, after decades of energy-efficiency gains and a shift towards less energy-intensive sectors, especially services; ECB analysis finds this has reduced the impact of oil supply shocks on growth, consumption and investment.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Lower oil intensity means smaller GDP sensitivity to oil spikes, so oil-shock recession playbooks calibrated on the 1970s-1990s overstate euro area downside.
insights.quote: The euro area economy is for example only half as reliant on oil as it was in the early 1990s
insights.locator: Is the economy less vulnerable to energy shocks?

insights.claim: A higher share of renewables reduces the share of hours in which gas-fired plants set the marginal electricity price, which lowers wholesale electricity prices and weakens the pass-through from wholesale gas to electricity prices.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The marginal-pricing mechanism is the key transmission channel: grids with high renewable penetration are structurally hedged against gas price spikes, which helps power-intensive industry in those countries.
insights.quote: a higher share of renewables reducing the share of hours in which gas-fired plants set the marginal price of electricity, decreasing the pass-through from wholesale gas to electricity prices
insights.locator: This shift is increasingly shaping electricity prices

insights.claim: In Spain the share of hours in which gas plants set electricity prices fell from around 80% in 2020 to just above 20% in 2026 (first nine months of each year), and in nuclear-heavy France it fell from around 60% to around 20%.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Spain and France now have power prices largely decoupled from gas, a relative competitiveness advantage over gas-marginal grids during gas shocks.
insights.quote: the share of hours in which gas plants set electricity prices has fallen from around 80% in 2020 to just above 20% in 2026
insights.locator: This shift is increasingly shaping electricity prices

insights.claim: Unlike the 2021-22 energy shock, when electricity prices closely tracked gas prices, the 2026 shock had a smaller impact on electricity prices in countries with larger renewable and nuclear shares during the first half of 2026.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Investors who expect 2022-style electricity price spikes from gas shocks are using an outdated template; the pass-through now varies widely by national generation mix.
insights.quote: Unlike during the 2021-22 energy shock, when electricity prices closely followed gas prices, the latest shock has had a smaller impact in countries with larger renewable and nuclear energy shares
insights.locator: This shift is increasingly shaping electricity prices

insights.claim: The link between higher low-carbon (nuclear plus renewable) generation and lower electricity prices is non-linear, so in some periods small changes in generation patterns can produce disproportionately lower or higher price responses.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Power price volatility can stay high even in low-carbon grids, which matters for pricing power derivatives and for utilities' merchant exposure.
insights.quote: small changes in the generation patterns can lead to a disproportionately lower or higher price response
insights.locator: The relationship between higher low-carbon

insights.claim: The expected euro area fiscal stance for 2026 doubled from an expansionary 0.25 percentage points in the December 2025 projections to 0.5 percentage points in later projections, which the authors describe as doubling expected fiscal support over 2026.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A fiscal impulse of 0.5pp of GDP is a meaningful growth support and partly offsets the energy drag, relevant for the ECB rate path and for Bund and periphery supply.
insights.quote: this has gradually increased to reach 0.5 percentage points, thus doubling the expected fiscal support for the euro area economy over 2026
insights.locator: At the same time, the public sector

insights.claim: The 2026 fiscal loosening mainly reflects higher defence and infrastructure spending in Germany, plus Next Generation EU-funded projects, strong growth in pensions and other social transfers, and temporary energy support measures of around 0.1% of GDP.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: German defence and infrastructure spending is the main driver of euro area fiscal expansion, supporting defence and construction exposures; energy subsidies themselves are small.
insights.quote: This mainly reflects higher spending on defence and infrastructure in Germany
insights.locator: At the same time, the public sector

insights.claim: Non-market (public) services have grown consistently above their long-term average and faster than other sectors in recent years, so a larger public sector has acted as a buffer against the energy shock.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Part of euro area GDP resilience comes from government activity rather than private demand, which tempers the read-through to corporate earnings.
insights.quote: non-market services have been consistently growing above their long-term average and faster than other sectors in recent years
insights.locator: At the same time, the public sector

insights.claim: Because part of the fiscal support is temporary, fiscal space is limited in several countries and projections show less fiscal support in coming years, fiscal policy may not be able to cushion further shocks to the same extent.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The next shock is likely to hit with a weaker fiscal backstop, which raises downside tail risk for euro area growth and spreads in fiscally constrained countries.
insights.quote: fiscal policy might not be able to cushion further shocks to the same extent
insights.locator: At the same time, the public sector

insights.claim: Global trade growth for 2026 is now projected at 4.7%, more than twice the 2% expected in the December 2025 Eurosystem projections, with strong AI-related trade an important driver of the upgrade.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A large upside surprise in world trade driven by the AI capex cycle has been a key export support for the open euro area economy.
insights.quote: the latest projections see global trade growth in 2026 as more than twice as high, at 4.7%
insights.locator: A second factor is that the global environment

insights.claim: As a highly open economy, the euro area benefited from stronger external demand for capital goods and specialised manufacturing products linked to AI-related investment, visible in PMI export orders for technology equipment.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: European capital-goods and specialised-equipment makers are AI-capex beneficiaries, so their earnings depend on global hyperscaler-style investment cycles.
insights.quote: the euro area benefited from stronger external demand for capital goods and specialised manufacturing products linked to AI-related investment
insights.locator: A second factor is that the global environment

insights.claim: Sectoral PMI data for January-September 2026 show that in technology equipment, the manufacturing subsector most linked to AI, output, employment and new orders developed considerably better than average, while the AI-exposed software services subsector outperformed on output but not on employment or new orders.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: AI is lifting hardware and equipment demand broadly, but in software it is raising output without hiring or order growth, consistent with AI productivity substituting for labour in services.
insights.quote: the software subsector, with its significant exposure to AI, performed better with respect to output but not with respect to employment and new orders
insights.locator: In technology equipment

insights.claim: Because demand in AI-related subsectors is so strong, a reversal of AI-related demand would leave parts of the euro area economy exposed.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: An AI capex downturn is now a macro risk for Europe as well as for US tech, which links European industrial cyclicals to AI-sentiment drawdowns.
insights.quote: a reversal in AI-related demand would leave parts of the economy exposed
insights.locator: In technology equipment

insights.claim: Production expectations collapsed and uncertainty spiked at the start of the Middle East conflict amid fears for energy and fertiliser supplies, but fears began fading as early as May and production expectations returned to pre-war levels in August and September once the worst scenarios failed to materialise.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Sentiment shocks from geopolitical events in the euro area have reverted within a few months when tail scenarios do not occur, which argues for buying sentiment troughs rather than extrapolating them.
insights.quote: When the worst conflict-related scenarios did not materialise, uncertainty receded and confidence returned
insights.locator: Uncertainty shot up after the start

insights.claim: Activity may have been temporarily boosted by precautionary behaviour, as some firms brought forward orders and production to secure supplies amid the risk of fuel shortages and higher costs.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Some 2026 activity may be pulled forward and could later reverse, a source of payback weakness in upcoming industrial data.
insights.quote: some firms may have brought forward orders and production to secure supplies
insights.locator: Uncertainty shot up after the start

insights.claim: Although large energy shocks have historically led to weaker labour demand and rising unemployment, euro area employment held up much better than expected in the first half of 2026 and kept growing, and PMI employment expectations quickly recovered to above pre-war levels, supporting incomes and consumption.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: A tight, resilient labour market supports consumer spending and keeps wage-driven inflation pressure in play, which makes deep ECB rate cuts less likely.
insights.quote: employment in the euro area held up much better than expected during the first half of the year and continued to expand
insights.locator: Finally, the labour market has provided

insights.claim: The euro area faces significant, interconnected downside risks that could materialise quickly: further geopolitical escalation, energy supply-chain disruption, worse financial market sentiment, renewed trade tensions and extreme weather, while the cushions of robust global demand, the AI investment boom and fiscal support may not persist at current levels.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The risk balance is skewed down just as the supports fade, so the ECB staff view leans toward vigilance rather than complacency about the growth outlook.
insights.quote: Several of these risks are interconnected and could materialise quickly.
insights.locator: Adaptive capacity: preparing for future shocks

insights.claim: The authors argue that further EU electricity market integration, with more cross-border interconnections and grid investment, would let cheaper renewable electricity flow where needed and reduce how far gas prices determine wholesale electricity prices.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Policy support for grids and interconnectors as an energy-security priority is a tailwind for European grid operators and transmission equipment suppliers.
insights.quote: Further integration of EU electricity markets, including more cross-border interconnections and investment in grids, would also help.
insights.locator: Adaptive capacity: preparing for future shocks

insights.claim: AI may create important growth and productivity opportunities for the euro area, but the scale and persistence of the benefits are uncertain and depend on how fast AI is adopted and diffused across firms and sectors.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: The ECB is not yet counting on an AI productivity boom, so diffusion metrics rather than capex are the indicator to watch for a lasting euro area growth upgrade.
insights.quote: the scale and persistence of these benefits remain uncertain and will depend on the speed of adoption and diffusion across firms and sectors
insights.locator: The second concerns innovation and technological change.

insights.claim: Rising financing needs from the energy and digital transitions require savings to be channelled more effectively to productive uses, so faster progress on a deeper savings and investments union would support both long-term growth and resilience.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Continued ECB pressure for capital-markets integration supports the case for deeper EU capital markets, which would benefit exchanges, asset managers and risk-capital providers.
insights.quote: Swifter progress towards a deeper savings and investments union could therefore support both long-term growth and resilience.
insights.locator: Finally, the third concerns the allocation of capital.
